Generating synthetic respondents in R

Source: vignettes/articles/generate.Rmd
generate.Rmd

This tutorial makes synthetic respondents from your own instrument, personas and models, in R code. The app does the same steps on screen, with or without real data. Synthetic respondents are for comparing models with the benchmark, or for pretesting a scale before real data exist, not for replacing a field test.

Everything below runs with the mock provider, which gives random answers without calling an API. Swap in sc_model("anthropic"), sc_model("openai") or sc_model("ollama", ...) for a real run.

library(synthcheck)

1. The instrument

sc_instrument() takes an item table (item, statement, and optionally scale, facet and reverse) or a plain vector of statements, plus the response scale:

ins <- sc_instrument(hexaco_items[hexaco_items$trait == "H", ], scale = c(1, 7),
                     name = "HEXACO Honesty-Humility")
ins
#> Instrument "HEXACO Honesty-Humility": 40 items, answers 1 to 7.
#> Scales: H 
#>   HSinc1: I don't pretend to be more than I am.
#>   HSinc2: I use flattery to get ahead.
#>   HSinc3: I tell other people what they want to hear so that they will do what I want them to do.
#>   ... and 37 more

Labels default to agree-disagree labels for 5- and 7-point scales. Give your own with labels, and your own text with instructions.

The bundled instruments come ready to use, with their response scale, labels and instructions: sc_builtin_instrument("rses") for the Rosenberg Self-Esteem Scale, "dass21" for the DASS-21, "mini_ipip" for the Mini-IPIP and "hexaco" for the IPIP-HEXACO. Each has real responses to compare with, and items with problems the literature already reports; see Short instruments with known item problems.

A template item table ships with the package:

tpl <- system.file("templates", "instrument_template.csv", package = "synthcheck")
read.csv(tpl)
#>   item                         statement             scale       facet reverse
#> 1   E1       I am the life of the party.      Extraversion Sociability   FALSE
#> 2   E2               I don't talk a lot.      Extraversion Sociability    TRUE
#> 3   E3 I feel comfortable around people.      Extraversion     Comfort   FALSE
#> 4   E4         I keep in the background.      Extraversion     Comfort    TRUE
#> 5   C1             I am always prepared. Conscientiousness       Order   FALSE
#> 6   C2     I leave my belongings around. Conscientiousness       Order    TRUE
#> 7   C3       I pay attention to details. Conscientiousness   Diligence   FALSE
#> 8   C4          I make a mess of things. Conscientiousness   Diligence    TRUE

2. The personas

A persona is the system prompt: Who the synthetic respondent is. Type them, or build every combination of a few attributes with sc_persona_grid():

per <- sc_persona_grid(age = c(25, 45, 65), gender = c("woman", "man"),
                       country = c("Canada", "the United States"),
                       template = "You are a {age}-year-old {gender} living in {country}.")
per
#> # A tibble: 12 × 5
#>    persona_id description                                     age gender country
#>    <chr>      <chr>                                         <dbl> <chr>  <chr>  
#>  1 p001       You are a 25-year-old woman living in Canada.    25 woman  Canada 
#>  2 p002       You are a 45-year-old woman living in Canada.    45 woman  Canada 
#>  3 p003       You are a 65-year-old woman living in Canada.    65 woman  Canada 
#>  4 p004       You are a 25-year-old man living in Canada.      25 man    Canada 
#>  5 p005       You are a 45-year-old man living in Canada.      45 man    Canada 
#>  6 p006       You are a 65-year-old man living in Canada.      65 man    Canada 
#>  7 p007       You are a 25-year-old woman living in the Un…    25 woman  the Un…
#>  8 p008       You are a 45-year-old woman living in the Un…    45 woman  the Un…
#>  9 p009       You are a 65-year-old woman living in the Un…    65 woman  the Un…
#> 10 p010       You are a 25-year-old man living in the Unit…    25 man    the Un…
#> 11 p011       You are a 45-year-old man living in the Unit…    45 man    the Un…
#> 12 p012       You are a 65-year-old man living in the Unit…    65 man    the Un…

The attribute columns are kept in the generated data, so you can compare groups later. sc_personas() takes a vector of descriptions or a table with a description column (see system.file("templates", "personas_template.csv", package = "synthcheck")).

3. The prompt

sc_prompt() shows exactly what is sent for one respondent:

p <- sc_prompt(ins, per$description[1], items = ins$items$item[1:3])
cat(p$system, "\n\n", p$user, sep = "")
#> You are a 25-year-old woman living in Canada.
#> 
#> You are taking part in a survey. Stay in this role and answer as this person would.
#> 
#> Please read each statement and decide how much you agree or disagree with it. There are no right or wrong answers. Answer every statement.
#> 
#> Answer with a whole number from 1 to 7:
#> 1 = Strongly disagree
#> 2 = Disagree
#> 3 = Slightly disagree
#> 4 = Neither agree nor disagree
#> 5 = Slightly agree
#> 6 = Agree
#> 7 = Strongly agree
#> 
#> Statements:
#> HSinc1: I don't pretend to be more than I am.
#> HSinc2: I use flattery to get ahead.
#> HSinc3: I tell other people what they want to hear so that they will do what I want them to do.
#> 
#> Return one answer for every statement, keyed by its name (HSinc1, HSinc2, ...).

The model answers in structured JSON, one whole number per item. Answers outside the scale and missing items are retried, then stored as NA.

4. The models 

sc_default_models
#> $anthropic
#> [1] "claude-haiku-5-5"
#> 
#> $openai
#> [1] "gpt-4.1-nano"
#> 
#> $ollama
#> NULL
#> 
#> $mock
#> [1] "mock"
sc_model("anthropic", temperature = 1)
#> claude-haiku-5-5 (anthropic, model "claude-haiku-5-5", temperature 1)
sc_model("ollama", "gemma3:27b", name = "Gemma 3 27B")
#> Gemma 3 27B (ollama, model "gemma3:27b", temperature 1)

The defaults are the cheapest models of each provider that take a temperature. temperature = NULL sends none, for models that do not take one. API keys come from ANTHROPIC_API_KEY and OPENAI_API_KEY (for example in .Renviron) and are never written to the saved files. New to API keys? Getting an API key walks through signing up, adding credit, keeping the key private and setting a spending limit.

5. Generate

An attempt is one full pass over the personas, with respondents respondents per persona. The number of calls is models × attempts × personas × respondents.

models <- list(sc_model("mock", name = "Mock A"), sc_model("mock", name = "Mock B"))
syn <- generate_synthetic(ins, models, per, attempts = 3, respondents = 10,
                          progress = FALSE, seed = 1)
dim(syn)
#> [1] 720  50
syn[1:3, 1:12]
#> # A tibble: 3 × 12
#>   model provider model_id temperature attempt persona_id respondent   age gender
#>   <chr> <chr>    <chr>          <dbl>   <int> <chr>           <int> <dbl> <chr> 
#> 1 Mock… mock     mock               1       1 p001                1    25 woman 
#> 2 Mock… mock     mock               1       1 p001                2    25 woman 
#> 3 Mock… mock     mock               1       1 p001                3    25 woman 
#> # ℹ 3 more variables: country <chr>, HSinc1 <int>, HSinc2 <int>

Useful settings for real runs:

  • parallel: How many calls run at the same time.
  • batch_size: Respondents per call. The default, 1, keeps every respondent independent. Larger batches are cheaper, but respondents in one call may depend on each other.
  • block_size: Items per call, for long instruments.
  • shuffle: A new item order for every respondent.
  • output: A folder. Each attempt is written there as soon as it is done, with the settings (run.json) and every prompt (prompts.json) beside it, so a stopped run keeps its finished attempts.
syn <- generate_synthetic(ins, list(sc_model("anthropic"), sc_model("openai")), per,
                          attempts = 5, respondents = 10, parallel = 8,
                          output = "hexaco_run")

What a run costs

estimate_cost() takes the same arguments and tells you what the run is likely to cost before you start it. It counts the calls, guesses their tokens from the prompts and multiplies them by the list prices in sc_prices. Ollama models are free, and so are calls already in the cache.

estimate_cost(ins, list(sc_model("anthropic"), sc_model("openai")), per,
              attempts = 5, respondents = 10, cache = FALSE)
#> Estimated cost: $0.20 for 1,200 calls.
#>  model            calls cached tokens_in tokens_out cost  prices_of 
#>  claude-haiku-5-5 600   0      644,400   99,000     $0.11 2026-11-03
#>  gpt-4.1-nano     600   0      452,400   99,000     $0.08 2026-02-18
#> An estimate: Tokens are guessed from the prompts, and retries add to it.

It is an estimate: Retries add to it, and reasoning models also bill their hidden reasoning. Prices change, so check them before a large run and pass your own table as prices when they differ (sc_prices has the date of each price in checked).

The response cache

Every answer is saved on disk, under a key made of the provider, the model, the temperature, the prompts, the respondent, the attempt and the seed. Running the same settings again reads the answers back instead of calling the models: The run is repeatable and costs nothing. More attempts or respondents call the models only for the new ones. A new seed asks again.

sc_cache_info()                       # what is saved, per model
syn <- generate_synthetic(..., cache = sc_cache(mode = "refresh"))   # ask again
syn <- generate_synthetic(..., cache = FALSE)                        # no cache
sc_cache_clear(model = "gpt-4.1-nano")                               # delete some

The cache lives in tools::R_user_dir("synthcheck", "cache"); give sc_cache("my_folder") to keep it with a project. It holds answers only, never API keys. cognitive_interview() uses it too, and estimate_interview_cost() estimates its cost.

6. Save and read 

f <- tempfile(fileext = ".csv")
write_synthetic(syn, f)
syn2 <- read_synthetic(f)
nrow(syn2)
#> [1] 720

read_synthetic() also reads a whole output folder back into one table.

7. Check the personas

A persona-based run assumes the model follows its personas. persona_fidelity() checks that. For each model and scale it measures how much of the scale score lies between personas (eta squared) and compares it with the same data after shuffling the persona labels. Add target_<scale> columns to the persona table (1 for high, 0 for average, -1 for low) to check the direction too:

per2 <- sc_personas(data.frame(
  description = c("You never bend the rules to get ahead and you dislike flattery.",
                  "You will say what people want to hear if it gets you what you want."),
  target_H = c(1, -1)))
syn_p <- generate_synthetic(ins, models[1], per2, respondents = 20, progress = FALSE)
fid <- persona_fidelity(syn_p, ins, per2)
fid
#> Persona check
#> 1 scale; scores standardized against each model's own respondents; 200 label shuffles.
#> 
#> Do personas separate respondents? (eta squared, against shuffled labels)
#>   model scale eta2 null    p separated
#>  Mock A     H 0.05 0.09 0.14     FALSE
#> 
#> Do they move in the intended direction?
#>   model persona  n targets  r  gap agree
#>  Mock A    p001 20       1 NA 1.21     0
#>  Mock A    p002 20       1 NA 1.21     0
#> 
#> Mock A: Personas do not change the scale scores more than shuffled labels do. The personas match the sign of 0% of their targets.
gg_persona_fidelity(fid)

The mock provider ignores personas, so its Honesty-Humility scores do not separate, and the personas miss their targets. A model that follows its personas separates them, with each persona on the side of its target. Give real to standardize the scores against real people, so a target of 1 means one standard deviation above them. The check shows whether a model follows its personas. It does not show that a persona answers like real people like it: The benchmark does that.

In the app, the Models tab shows the same check after a run with two or more personas.

8. Benchmark

as_synthetic_list() turns the long table into the list of models and attempts that the benchmark takes:

real <- hexaco_real[hexaco_real$country == "Canada", ]
bm <- authenticity_benchmark(as_synthetic_list(syn, items = ins$items$item), real, ins$items,
                             fit_scales = character(0), n_splits = 5, n_floor = 5)
bm
#> Synthetic authenticity benchmark
#> 40 items, 1708 real respondents. Score: weakest.
#> 
#>   model attempts Overlap Structure Behaviour Score Score 95%   Weakest
#>  Mock B        3       2         1        -3    -3  -13 to 1 Behaviour
#>  Mock A        3      -9        -1         8    -9  -25 to 1   Overlap
#> 
#> Anchors (raw, floor to ceiling, samples of 120): Overlap 51.5 to 85.0, Structure 79.0 to 89.5, Behaviour 66.4 to 85.1.
#> 0 = shuffled real columns, 100 = a second sample of real people.
summarise_benchmark(bm)
#> Synthetic authenticity benchmark in plain language
#> 
#> Mock B scores -3 on the benchmark (1st of 2), set by its weakest
#> column, Behaviour. Its 95% interval runs from -13 to 1. It overlaps
#> with that of Mock A, so the data do not clearly separate the two.
#> Overlap is 2 (barely better than shuffled columns); Structure is 1
#> (barely better than shuffled columns); Behaviour is -3 (worse than
#> shuffled columns). Compared with real people, they give more extreme
#> answers (behaviour overlap 50) and their answers vary more across items
#> (behaviour overlap 54).
#> 
#> Mock A scores -9 on the benchmark (2nd of 2), set by its weakest
#> column, Overlap. Its 95% interval runs from -25 to 1. Overlap is -9
#> (worse than shuffled columns); Structure is -1 (worse than shuffled
#> columns); Behaviour is 8 (barely better than shuffled columns).
#> Compared with real people, they give more extreme answers (behaviour
#> overlap 49) and their answers vary more across items (behaviour overlap
#> 53).
#> 
#> 100 = as close as a second sample of real people; 0 = no better than shuffled columns.

Random answers score close to 0 on every column, as they should: 0 is what shuffled real answers score. Real language models are not guaranteed to do better. On HEXACO, the six models in hexaco_llm often fall below 0 because their respondents bunch together; see the benchmark.

9. A report

write_report() puts the results in one file: The plots, the tables, the plain-language summaries and the settings needed to repeat the run. HTML (the default) is one self-contained file that opens in any browser. PDF uses R’s own PDF device, so it needs no LaTeX.

write_report(list(benchmark = bm, synthetic = syn, instrument = ins,
                  personas = per, models = models), "my_report.html")
write_report(bm, "my_report.pdf")

A pretest (synthetic_pretest()) and cognitive interviews (cognitive_interview()) go in the same way, as pretest and interviews. The app’s Export tab downloads the same report.
